player.name: Wren Ashdown
player.concept: a quick-witted half-elf ranger with a longbow, a dry sense of humour and a soft spot for underdogs

established: Garrow has admitted that Tam Hollis was telling the truth about the goblins.
canon: The hole’s splinters flare inward, and the tip of something black is lodged in the wood.
Wren has unstrung the longbow and bound it with their own cord; Garrow has not accepted that as a formal peace-bond.

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
The King's Road dips over a humpbacked stone bridge, the winter river below it roaring brown and swollen. Beside the bridge, a whitewashed toll house smokes beneath crooked Centennial bunting. A grey goose patrols the striped bar, hissing as Garrow steps out with the ledger under his arm. He lowers the bar with grave ceremony, though the road is empty in both directions. A small, fresh splintered hole marks the door behind him.

“On foot: the King’s penny, one silver. The Assembly levy, twelve pennies. And your longbow, borne on the King’s Road: two pennies under Marshal Holt’s order. Fifteen pennies in all.” Garrow writes each item with relish, then poises his pencil over the ledger. “Your names and business, travellers?”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I step up to the bar, produce a small notebook and a stub of pencil of my own, and match his gravity exactly. "Wren Ashdown, ranger. Business: attendance at the Centennial Assembly, in a private capacity. Now, before any coin changes hands, I shall require an itemised receipt, in triplicate, and sight of Marshal Holt's order. The original, with the seal, not a copy. And a point of clarification for the record: is the bow levy assessed per bow, or per string? Because I carry a spare string, and I should hate to be in arrears."

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Garrow’s pencil pauses at “private capacity.” At the question of the string, he looks over his spectacles.

“Per weapon, not per string. I have not yet had occasion to tax spare strings.”

He taps the arms notice with one ink-stained finger. “There is the order. It is posted, and the Marshal’s seal is upon the notice. I have no original to hand you. Nor, I’m afraid, do I keep a triplicate receipt service at the bar.”

His eyes flick to your notebook. A reluctant glint of respect warms his expression. “But you may inspect the order and the Book, and I can write you a receipt. One copy. Shall I enter ‘one bow, one weapon’?”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I nod gravely. "One bow, one weapon. Entered under protest, if you please, pending appeal." I step to the arms notice and read it very closely, nose almost to the parchment, checking the seal, the date and the wording, and copying the key clause into my notebook. Then I turn and point my pencil at the fresh splintered hole in the door behind him. "And while we are on the Book. That is damage to a Crown toll house. Has it been entered? There ought to be an incident report. Date, time, nature of damage, suspected party. I would be happy to witness it."

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
You copy the arms order’s wording: “two pennies a weapon; peace-bonded weapons free.” The seal is genuine, the date current. Garrow watches you finish with an aggrieved little sniff.

At your question, his eyes dart to the hole. “Damage?” He shifts the ledger against his chest. “A cart-shaft, most likely. Or a knot in the timber. The door is sound.”

The goose gives a low, suspicious honk. Garrow flinches before he can stop himself, then scowls at it. “It is not an incident. Nothing to enter.” His pencil hovers over the page. “And I do not require a witness for routine maintenance.”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I tap my notebook. "Peace-bonded weapons free. Then I elect to peace-bond." I unstring the longbow, take a length of cord from my pack, and bind the bow and string together with a neat, tight knot, then hold it out to him. "One weapon, peace-bonded in the presence of the toll-keeper. Kindly enter it and amend my assessment to thirteen pennies." While he considers that, I lean past him and look at the hole properly, the way I would read a track: which way the splinters are pushed, how high it sits, whether anything is still lodged in the wood. "A cart-shaft, at that height, on a door, with the road empty both ways. Remarkable cart."

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Garrow draws breath to answer, then finds no words for the height of the hole. Your close look shows the splinters flare inward; the tip of something black still catches in the wood. His fingers tighten on the ledger.

“Peace-bonding is properly done with red cord and my seal,” he says, stiffly. “Your own cord does not amend the charge.” Yet he doesn’t reach for the bow. His gaze has gone past you, across the road to the blackthorn hedge.

The goose hisses at a stirring twig. Garrow jumps, then looks furious with himself. “Tam was drunk,” he says, too quickly. “It is entered in the ledger.” He retreats a step toward the half-door. “The toll remains thirteen pennies.”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I draw my knife and, with great care, work the black tip out of the door, then fold it into a page torn from my notebook and write on the outside in block capitals: EXHIBIT A. RECOVERED FROM CROWN PROPERTY. CHAIN OF CUSTODY: W. ASHDOWN. I look at what it is before I seal it. Then, without raising my voice and without looking at the hedge, I say to Garrow: "Thirteen pennies, you said. I accept the assessment. Now. Tam was drunk, and Tam was entered. Is Tam the one in the hedge, or is it whoever owns this?"

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
The black tip is an arrowhead, chipped stone bound to a short, black-fletched shaft. Garrow watches you wrap it; his denial falls away.

“No. Tam wasn’t in the hedge.” He swallows, eyes fixed on the exhibit in your hand. “The arrow came after he left. I pulled it out and hid it in the drawer.”

He opens the half-door, but doesn’t reach for the ledger. “He told me there were goblins on the road. I laughed at him. Fined him, too.” His voice goes thin. “I was wrong.”

Across the road, the blackthorn stirs in the wind. Garrow looks at the tracks beneath it, then back at you. “There’s a clause in the Book for true reports of peril. I should have listened.”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: "Then we shall do this properly." I tuck Exhibit A into my jerkin. "Find the clause and read it to me, word for word. If Tam made a true report of peril and was fined for it, that fine is void and the report must be entered, with the arrow in your drawer as Exhibit B. Precedent matters, Garrow. The next man to see goblins needs to know he will be believed and not charged a penny for the privilege." Then I cross the road, crouch by the blackthorn, and read the tracks underneath it: how many, which way, how fresh.

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Garrow fumbles the chained Book open, keeping one finger on the page as though the words might escape.

“Clause of Perils,” he reads, voice tight. “‘A traveller who brings the warden true report of peril upon the Road passes free of toll, and the warden shall send word to the Marshal at Caerwyn without delay.’” He looks up. “Tam’s two pennies, too. I’ll return them. They’re in the drawer—with the arrow.”

He watches you cross to the hedge, but doesn’t leave the bar. Beneath the blackthorn, the small clawed tracks are pressed into frozen mud, sharp-edged and fresh. You can make out several, overlapping; they lead away from the road and vanish into the hedge. Wind stirs the bare branches above them.

Behind you, Garrow says, “I have no men to send. I’ll have to write to the Marshal myself.” His hand closes around the Book’s chain. “And put my own name in the account.”
